My thesis asks whether reinforcement learning can turn information in the order

## Can order-book information become a trading edge? {#method data-timing="45"}

::: {.kicker}
Research question & method
:::

::: {.lead}
Learn **how much to hold** from the state of the market.
:::

::::: {.flow}
::: {.flow-node}

Ten microstructure features:<br>
imbalance, depth, flow,<br>
spread and volatility
:::
::: {.flow-arrow aria-hidden="true"}
→
:::

<h3>Learn</h3>

A policy proposes exposure;<br>
two critics assess it
:::
::: {.flow-arrow aria-hidden="true"}
→
:::
::: {.flow-node}
<h3>Act</h3>

Continuous exposure<br>

::: {.assumptions}

:::

::: {.source}
Source: thesis, Chapters 4–5. TD3 = Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient.
:::

::: {.folio}
02 / 07
:::

::: {.notes}
**45 seconds · cumulative 1:05**

The order book records supply and demand close to the current price. I represent
it with ten selected features, including imbalance, depth, trade flow, spread,
and volatility. The agent chooses a continuous position between fully short
and fully long, rather than only a buy-or-sell decision. TD3 uses a policy
network and two value networks to learn that choice. Its Differential Sharpe
reward makes the balance between return and risk part of training. The baseline
is deliberately frictionless: trades are valued at the midpoint, with no fee,
delay, or market impact. Those assumptions are central to interpreting the results.
:::

::: {.notes}
**40 seconds · cumulative 1:45**

The data cover six liquid Nasdaq equities over four trading sessions. Training
uses the first three sessions. Each instrument's fourth session is split
chronologically into validation and test halves by event count. This leaves
about three point seven million test observations. The model is pooled across
instruments, but controls one position at a time; this is not a six-asset
portfolio. Features use past-only running normalization. The split preserves
time order, but millions of events should not be confused with a broad sample
of market conditions: the test still covers only part of one session.
:::

::: {.folio}
04 / 07
:::

::: {.notes}
**50 seconds · cumulative 2:35**

I first ask whether training changes performance relative to random actions.
The chart shows profit factor: gross gains divided by absolute gross losses.
One means those gains and losses balance. TD3 reaches about three point four,
while the random policy remains close to one. DDPG and PPO also perform well.
These are averages across the same six instrument tests, under the same
frictionless assumptions. The useful conclusion is that learned actions differ
from random actions in this simulator. It is not proof of a deployable edge,
and it does not identify TD3 as the best algorithm. With one seed per
configuration and one short test window, the ranking is descriptive.
:::

## Estimated spread costs overturn the result {#execution data-timing="65"}

::: {.kicker}
Economic test · The same TD3 action path
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="64%"}
```{python}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: 100%
#| fig-alt: "Estimated spread cost divided by gross profit for six equities. Each bar is labelled with its ratio; the dashed line marks cost equal to profit."
bar_chart(
    [r["symbol"] for r in spread], ratios,
    colours=[BURGUNDY] * len(spread),
    axis="Estimated spread cost / gross profit · times",
    limit=44, breaks=[0, 10, 20, 30, 40], digits=1, suffix="×",
)
```
:::
::: {.column width="33%" .result-aside}
::: {.big}
`{python} f"{min(ratios):.0f}–{max(ratios):.0f}×"`
:::

spread cost relative<br>to gross profit

**`{python} negative_count` of `{python} len(spread)` instruments turn negative.**

::: {.small}
Estimated cost = total absolute position change × mean relative half-spread.

Fixed policy; no retraining.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.source}
Source: thesis §7.2.1 and appendix bid/ask repricing export. Mean-spread approximation, not a fill-by-fill execution simulation. Dashed line: cost = profit.
:::

::: {.folio}
05 / 07
:::

::: {.notes}
**65 seconds · cumulative 3:40**

The economic test is what happens when we charge for the trading that this
policy requires. A trade at the midpoint avoids paying the spread between the
best buy and sell prices. The thesis estimates the missing cost by multiplying
the policy's total absolute position changes by each instrument's mean relative
half-spread. The chart divides that cost by gross profit. The dashed line at one
is where cost would exactly absorb the profit. Every instrument lies far beyond
it: costs are roughly fifteen to thirty-eight times the gross profit, and all
six results turn negative. This is an approximation using the mean spread,
not a simulation of individual fills. Crucially, it keeps the action path fixed.
It therefore challenges this frictionlessly trained policy, without showing
what a policy trained with realistic costs could achieve. That distinction
leads directly to the next experiment.
:::

:::

::: {.folio}
06 / 07
:::

::: {.notes}
**40 seconds · cumulative 4:20**

The robustness experiments add an important qualification. When agents are
trained separately at different fees, the two lowest-fee runs trade actively,
while the higher-fee runs settle into static positions. This shows cost
sensitivity, but does not locate the break-even fee of a functioning strategy.
The feature and reward comparisons remain unresolved. Only the selected
feature set and Differential Sharpe reward produced trading policies in their
respective comparisons. The other runs failed to train. Those failures identify
training stability as a problem to solve; they do not establish that the
alternative features or objective are intrinsically worse.
:::

The contribution is a reproducible research pipeline and a clear economic

assumptions, but that policy cannot cover estimated spread-crossing costs.
The study does not establish live profitability or reliable performance across
market regimes. The next step is to retrain with explicit bid and ask execution,
then address stability across seeds and test across more sessions. That would
separate a robust, cost-aware trading policy from a result that depends on the
simulator. Thank you.

## Appendix · Matched H1 results {#appendix-results .backup}

::: {.kicker}
Questions only · Outside the five-minute talk
:::

```{python}
#| output: asis
rows = ["| Algorithm | Gross return | Max drawdown | Profit factor | Turnover |",
        "|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|"]
for name, m in h1.items():
    rows.append(f"| {name} | {m['total_return']:.2%} | {m['max_drawdown']:.2%} | "
                f"{m['profit_factor']:.2f} | {m['turnover']:.3f} |")
display(Markdown("\n".join(rows)))
```

::: {.small}
**Aggregation:** equal-weight means of six separate instrument evaluations;<br>
these are not returns on a jointly traded six-asset portfolio.

**Gross return:** compounded over the test window, before execution costs.<br>
**Turnover:** mean absolute position change per event.

The random control is a useful diagnostic; it does not rule out every source of bias.
:::

::: {.source}
Source: committed H1 evaluation_report.json for TD3, DDPG, PPO and Random; thesis §6.1. Same per-symbol event counts for all four algorithms.
:::

::: {.folio}
A1
:::

::: {.notes}
Use this table if asked about return, drawdown, turnover, or algorithm choice.
These are stored thesis metrics, not newly computed results. Profit factor is
averaged across symbols, so dividing pooled gross profit by pooled gross loss
will not generally reproduce it. Very large gross cumulative returns are
conditional on frictionless execution and a large number of compounded events.
:::

## Appendix · What the spread estimate measures {#appendix-costs .backup}

::: {.kicker}
Questions only · Fixed-path sensitivity
:::

```{python}
#| output: asis
rows = ["| Instrument | Break-even fee (bp) | Mean half-spread (bp) | Cost / profit |",
        "|:--|--:|--:|--:|"]
for r in spread:
    rows.append(f"| {r['symbol']} | {r['breakeven_fee_bp']:.3f} | "
                f"{r['half_spread_bp_mean']:.3f} | {r['cost_to_profit_ratio']:.1f}× |")
display(Markdown("\n".join(rows)))
```

::: {.small}
**Break-even fee:** summed gross simple-return contributions / total absolute position changes.

Fixed-path estimate using a mean spread; separate from H2 retraining.<br>
Individual fills, queue position, fees, latency and impact are not modelled.
:::

::: {.source}
Source: committed peek/bid_ask_repricing.json; scripts/export_bid_ask_repricing_to_thesis.py. Values use the same fixed TD3 path as the main chart.
:::

::: {.folio}
A2
:::

::: {.notes}
The break-even fee here belongs to the fixed action path. It is expressed per
unit of absolute position change. It is not the threshold identified by the
fee sweep, because that sweep trains different policies. The calculation adds
simple-return contributions; it does not compound an executable net equity
curve or impose insolvency. A full execution model would use contemporaneous
bid/ask quotes for each position change and retrain with those costs.
:::

## Appendix · Why this method? {#appendix-method .backup}

::: {.kicker}
Questions only · Design choices & remaining controls
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
<h3>Why TD3?</h3>

- Continuous actions preserve the exposure-sizing decision.
- Twin critics, delayed policy updates, and target smoothing aim to stabilize learning.
- The empirical comparison does **not** establish superiority over DDPG or PPO.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
<h3>Why Differential Sharpe?</h3>

- Running return moments supply an online, risk-adjusted training signal.
- Financial metrics are evaluated separately from the shaped reward.
- The log-return run's collapse leaves reward quality unresolved.
:::
::::

::: {.next-step .small}
**Additional controls:** more seeds and sessions; a non-RL model on the same
features; realistic execution and delay.
:::

::: {.source}
Source: thesis Chapters 3–4 and §7.2. Technical derivations and citations remain in the thesis; this appendix summarizes the design rationale.
:::

::: {.folio}
A3
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not defend TD3 as uniquely necessary: the results do not support that claim.
Its selection was a design choice for continuous control. A supervised or
linear-policy baseline on the same feature set would better isolate the
contribution of reinforcement learning itself. Additional seeds are needed to
separate systematic training problems from sensitivity to initialization.
:::
